Please solve this issue: Our test suite grew big and we haven't noticed how the total RSpec run time outgrew 10 minutes (no parallelization) on CI.

We need to profile the test suite and identify the common problems (shared by many specs) and fix them once and for all. Keep refactoring of individual examples minimal: prefer configuration- and setup-level changes — adding tags, restructuring shared setup, wrapping execution. What the examples assert must stay the same. No app code changes affecting runtime behavior.

NOTE: Running the whole test suite is very time-consuming. Don't try to run the whole test suite (it would fail with timeout due to the Bash tool limitations) or even multiple directories. Only `rspec spec/<some-folder>`. Completely ignore system specs and streaming related specs (we do not run them by default anyway).

We will work on specific spec types at each optimization phase: `spec/models` and `spec/requests`. In the end, we want these two groups together to run at least twice as fast as they do today. Store any insights/comments/plans (such as baseline metrics) that could be useful for the future runs in the docs/ folder (so you can use that knowledge during future optimization runs).

Let's start with `spec/models`—don't touch other spec types during this step.
Also, do not touch factories yet — we will work on them later.

At least a 30-35% speed improvement for `spec/models` is expected; however, don't hesitate to squeeze more if you see an opportunity (aka low-hanging fruits).

--require spec_helper
--- .env.test ---
# In test, compile the NodeJS code as if we are in production
NODE_ENV=production
# Federation
LOCAL_DOMAIN=cb6e6126.ngrok.io
LOCAL_HTTPS=true

# Secret values required by ActiveRecord encryption feature
# Use `bin/rails db:encryption:init` to generate fresh secrets
ACTIVE_RECORD_ENCRYPTION_DETERMINISTIC_KEY=test_determinist_key_DO_NOT_USE_IN_PRODUCTION
ACTIVE_RECORD_ENCRYPTION_KEY_DERIVATION_SALT=test_salt_DO_NOT_USE_IN_PRODUCTION
ACTIVE_RECORD_ENCRYPTION_PRIMARY_KEY=test_primary_key_DO_NOT_USE_IN_PRODUCTION
--- spec_helper.rb ---
# frozen_string_literal: true

if ENV.fetch('COVERAGE', false)
  require 'simplecov'
  SimpleCov.start 'rails'
end

RSpec.configure do |config|
  config.example_status_persistence_file_path = 'tmp/rspec/examples.txt'
  config.expect_with :rspec do |expectations|
    expectations.include_chain_clauses_in_custom_matcher_descriptions = true
  end

  config.disable_monkey_patching!

  config.mock_with :rspec do |mocks|
    mocks.verify_partial_doubles = true
  end

  config.before :suite do
    Rails.application.load_seed
    Chewy.strategy(:bypass)

    # NOTE: we switched registrations mode to closed by default, but the specs
    # very heavily rely on having it enabled by default, as it relies on users
    # being approved by default except in select cases where explicitly testing
    # other registration modes
    Setting.registrations_mode = 'open'
  end

  config.after :suite do
    FileUtils.rm_rf(Rails.root.glob('spec/test_files'))
  end

  # Use the GitHub Annotations formatter for CI
  if ENV['GITHUB_ACTIONS'] == 'true' && ENV['GITHUB_RSPEC'] == 'true'
    require 'rspec/github'
    config.add_formatter RSpec::Github::Formatter
  end
end

def serialized_record_json(record, serializer, adapter: nil, options: {})
  options[:serializer] = serializer
  options[:adapter] = adapter if adapter.present?
  JSON.parse(
    ActiveModelSerializers::SerializableResource.new(
      record,
      options
    ).to_json
  )
end
--- rails_helper.rb ---
# frozen_string_literal: true

ENV['RAILS_ENV'] ||= 'test'

# This needs to be defined before Rails is initialized

ENV['STREAMING_API_BASE_URL'] = "http://#{STREAMING_HOST}:#{STREAMING_PORT}"

require_relative '../config/environment'

abort('The Rails environment is running in production mode!') if Rails.env.production?

module BrowserErrorsHelpers
  def ignore_js_error(error)
    @ignored_js_errors_for_spec << error
  end

  def error_message(error)
    error.keys.map { |key| "#{key.to_s.titleize}: #{error[key]}" }.join("\n")
  end
end

RSpec.configure do |config|
  config.include BrowserErrorsHelpers, :js, type: :system

  config.before(:each, :js, type: :system) do |example|
    @ignored_js_errors_for_spec = []

    example.metadata[:js_console_messages] ||= []
    Capybara.current_session.driver.with_playwright_page do |page|
      page.on('console', lambda { |msg|
        example.metadata[:js_console_messages] << { type: msg.type, text: msg.text, location: msg.location, page: msg.page.url }
      })
    end
  end

  config.after(:each, :js, type: :system) do |example|
    # Classes of intermittent ignorable errors
    ignored_errors = [
      /Error while trying to use the following icon from the Manifest/, # https://github.com/mastodon/mastodon/pull/30793
      /Manifest: Line: 1, column: 1, Syntax error/, # Similar parsing/interruption issue as above
    ].concat(@ignored_js_errors_for_spec)

    errors = example.metadata[:js_console_messages].reject do |msg|
      ignored_errors.any? { |pattern| pattern.match(msg[:text]) }
    end

    if errors.present?
      aggregate_failures 'browser errrors' do
        errors.each do |error|
          expect(error[:type]).to_not eq('error'), error_message(error)
          next unless error[:type] == 'warning'

          warn 'WARN: browser warning'
          warn error[:text]
        end
      end
    end
  end
end

module DomainHelpers
  def configure_mx(domain:, exchange:, ip_v4_addr: '2.3.4.5', ip_v6_addr: 'fd00::2')
    resolver = instance_double(Resolv::DNS, :timeouts= => nil)

      .with(domain, Resolv::DNS::Resource::IN::AAAA)

module BrowserErrorsHelpers
  def ignore_js_error(error)
    @ignored_js_errors_for_spec << error
  end

  def error_message(error)
    error.keys.map { |key| "#{key.to_s.titleize}: #{error[key]}" }.join("\n")
  end
end

RSpec.configure do |config|
  config.include BrowserErrorsHelpers, :js, type: :system

  config.before(:each, :js, type: :system) do |example|
    @ignored_js_errors_for_spec = []

    example.metadata[:js_console_messages] ||= []
    Capybara.current_session.driver.with_playwright_page do |page|
      page.on('console', lambda { |msg|
        example.metadata[:js_console_messages] << { type: msg.type, text: msg.text, location: msg.location, page: msg.page.url }
      })
    end
  end

  config.after(:each, :js, type: :system) do |example|
    # Classes of intermittent ignorable errors
    ignored_errors = [
      /Error while trying to use the following icon from the Manifest/, # https://github.com/mastodon/mastodon/pull/30793
      /Manifest: Line: 1, column: 1, Syntax error/, # Similar parsing/interruption issue as above
    ].concat(@ignored_js_errors_for_spec)

    errors = example.metadata[:js_console_messages].reject do |msg|
      ignored_errors.any? { |pattern| pattern.match(msg[:text]) }
    end

    if errors.present?
      aggregate_failures 'browser errrors' do
        errors.each do |error|
          expect(error[:type]).to_not eq('error'), error_message(error)
          next unless error[:type] == 'warning'

          warn 'WARN: browser warning'
          warn error[:text]
        end
      end
    end
  end
end

**Filtering Out the Noise**

Alright, that's a classic! I see what happened – the globbing pattern, probably used for a `require` statement or something similar, ended up matching something way outside its intended scope. Specifically, I'm thinking about how `/usr/local/bundle/...` ended up colliding with `/lib/`. That's a textbook example of a pathing problem.

So, to tighten things up and avoid these kinds of unintended matches in the future, I'm going to implement some very strict filtering. I'll focus exclusively on these three directories: `Dir.pwd + "/app/"`, `Dir.pwd + "/lib/"`, and `Dir.pwd + "/spec/"`. messages.thinking:
**Analyzing Sidekiq Performance in Model Specs**

Okay, let's break this down. My initial concern stems from the `WebhookService#call` method and the configuration in `rails_helper.rb`.  I see that whenever a `Status`, `User`, `Report`, `Follow`, or `Account` is created or updated, an `after_commit` hook enqueues a `TriggerWebhookWorker`.  The problem is, because `rails_helper.rb` uses `Sidekiq.testing!(:inline)`, this worker executes synchronously *immediately* on EVERY model change during testing.

Furthermore, `WebhookService#call` then goes on to execute `serialize_event`, which apparently constructs a heavy JSON payload using `REST::Admin::WebhookEventSerializer`.  This involves queries on `AccountStat`, `REST::Admin::AccountSerializer`, `FormattingHelper` and takes around 30ms per call. The kicker? This entire process happens even if `Webhook.enabled` is empty, indicating a potential performance bottleneck. This likely indicates some N+1 problems in this system.

This makes me question what *other* Sidekiq workers are being triggered inline during model spec runs.  It's a huge potential performance drain that I need to investigate further.

The solution seems to be using `TestProf`'s built-in custom events: `sidekiq.inline` and `sidekiq.jobs`.  I remember seeing the relevant files in the `test-prof` gem: `/usr/local/bundle/gems/test-prof-1.6.3/lib/test_prof/event_prof/custom_events/sidekiq_inline.rb` and `/usr/local/bundle/gems/test-prof-1.6.3/lib/test_prof/event_prof/custom_events/sidekiq_jobs.rb`.

My next step is to run `EVENT_PROF="sidekiq.inline"` and `EVENT_PROF="sidekiq.jobs"` on the `spec/models` suite. **Uncovering Performance Bottlenecks in `spec/models`**

Okay, hold on a second. This is significant. We've stumbled upon a couple of incredibly wasteful behaviors in our model specs. First, the `account_fabricator.rb` is creating a `User` every single time it fabricates an `Account`, triggering a cascade of operations – bcrypt hashing, login activities, approval checks, and webhooks – even when the spec might not need any of that user-related setup. This is repeated 1,194 times in `spec/models`, so is a considerable overhead.

Second, the `status_fabricator.rb` is *also* creating a `bookmark`, which in turn creates *another* `account` and *another* `user` every single time a `status` is created. This seems totally unnecessary.

Ah, that explains the prompt's warning to hold off on factory changes! Clearly, the plan is to tackle factories later, in their own dedicated phase. That gives us a very clear direction for *this* phase: we *must* avoid touching `spec/fabricators/`!

So, what's on the optimization table for *this* phase? Configuration and setup-level changes within `spec/models` and `rails_helper.rb`. The goal is to identify and address the root causes of slow tests, focusing on shared setup, structure, and execution wrapping, without modifying the core behavior of our application's code or individual examples. We are looking for common problems that apply across many specs.

Now, we need to dig deeper. We know bcrypt hashing is contributing 4.7% of the total time (1.15s out of 23s) due to generating passwords. Let's look at `config/initializers/devise.rb` to understand how the test environment is configured. Aha! The bcrypt cost is set to 1 for the test environment, which is the minimum value. However, the problem isn't the cost itself (it's already the minimum), but the *number of times* it's being called, which is twice per `Status` due to the cascading fabrications: `account` -> `user` -> `bookmark` -> `account` -> `user`. The bcrypt cost itself cannot be lowered. We shouldn't mock bcrypt, because it is an integral part of the password authentication specs.

messages.thinking:
**Analyzing Test Suite Bottlenecks for Optimization**

Okay, I'm diving in. My initial scan of individual spec files, like `account_statuses_cleanup_policy_spec.rb` and `tag_feed_spec.rb`, revealed obvious inefficiencies. We have redundant object creation and unnecessary database interactions across multiple examples. The `trends/statuses_spec.rb` file reinforces this pattern. However, as the instructions clearly stated, we're not going to drastically alter the individual tests. The focus needs to be on identifying and fixing *common* problems at a configuration or setup level to realize global performance gains.

First, I need to check `spec/models`, `rails_helper.rb`, `spec_helper.rb` and `config/environments/test.rb` for these shared pain points. Let's make a list.

1.  **`TriggerWebhookWorker` and WebhookService:** A significant chunk of time, roughly 25% of the total runtime, is being consumed by inline execution of the `TriggerWebhookWorker`. This is happening even when no webhooks are enabled. It looks like many jobs are unnecessarily running due to callbacks on the `Status`, `User`, and `Account` models, and so on. We can fix this! Let's examine how to stub or disable `TriggerWebhookWorker` when no webhooks are needed. We need to be careful to only enable it in a specific, tagged, scenario, to cover all code paths. The instructions say we should not change app code. So how do we make this work?

    *   I'll analyze `spec/support/` to create a new module, and then add to `rails_helper.rb` or `spec/support/disable_webhooks.rb` to disable unless the `webhooks` tag is present.
    *   I will examine if any specs *do* rely on `TriggerWebhookWorker` firing and ensure we enable it there with the tag.

2.  **Global Overheads in `spec/models`**:

    a)  **Database Queries, SQL Logging, Cache Clearing, and Route Reloading:** It is important to see the performance of these shared elements and figure out a way to optimize them.

        *   I will measure the time taken by the `config.before` and `config.after` hooks in `rails_helper.rb`. We need to determine how much of the runtime is spent reloading routes on every test, clearing the cache, and deleting Redis keys.
        *   I also need to see if the RSpec mock setup overhead, specifically the `allow(Resolv::DNS).to receive(:open)` stub, and corresponding teardown, are a bottleneck.
        *   The frequent `redis.del(redis.keys)` calls are probably expensive. I'll test `FLUSHDB` vs. `DEL` and see if there is an easy win here.
        *   I'm also seeing repeated calls to expensive methods like `User#set_approved`, `UsernameBlock.matches?`, `EmailDomainBlock.requires_approval?`, `UserRole.everyone`, and `Setting.[]`. These seem to be eating up a lot of time. The fact that the cache is being cleared on every example *definitely* explains why these methods are taking ~15% of the total runtime.

    b)  **ActiveRecord SQL Logging Overhead:** This is a BIG one. The StackProf output shows that a significant amount of time is spent in `ActiveRecord::LogSubscriber#sql`. If we are logging DEBUG SQL to a file for every one of the 114,000 SQL queries, this is hugely inefficient. It's time to check `config/environments/test.rb` to see if we can reduce this logging, maybe even disable it for tests.

    c)  **Other ActiveSupport, Devise, BCrypt, Chewy, and Instrumentation Overheads:** We also need to check these for potential issues. The goal is to identify all the bottlenecks.

Next, I'll execute a command to inspect `config/application.rb`, `config/environments/test.rb` (logging level), and all the models that are being referenced again and again like `UserRole.everyone`, `Setting`, `UsernameBlock`, and `EmailDomainBlock` and measure the performance.

{
  "returncode": 0,
  "output": "# frozen_string_literal: true

# Set OTEL_* environment variables according to OTel docs:
# https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/sdk-configuration/

if ENV.keys.any? { |name| name.match?(/OTEL_.*_ENDPOINT/) }
  require 'opentelemetry/sdk'
  require 'opentelemetry/exporter/otlp'

  require 'opentelemetry/instrumentation/active_job'
  require 'opentelemetry/instrumentation/active_model_serializers'
  require 'opentelemetry/instrumentation/concurrent_ruby'
  require 'opentelemetry/instrumentation/excon'
  require 'opentelemetry/instrumentation/faraday'
  require 'opentelemetry/instrumentation/http'
  require 'opentelemetry/instrumentation/http_client'
  require 'opentelemetry/instrumentation/net/http'
  require 'opentelemetry/instrumentation/pg'
  require 'opentelemetry/instrumentation/rack'
  require 'opentelemetry/instrumentation/rails'
  require 'opentelemetry/instrumentation/redis'
  require 'opentelemetry/instrumentation/sidekiq'

  OpenTelemetry::SDK.configure do |c|
    # use_all() attempts to load ALL the auto-instrumentations
    # currently loaded by Ruby requires.
    #
    # Load attempts will emit an INFO or WARN to the console
    # about the success/failure to wire up an auto-instrumentation.
    # "WARN -- : Instrumentation: <X> failed to install" is most
    # likely caused by <X> not being a Ruby library loaded by
    # the application or the instrumentation has been explicitly
    # disabled.
    #
    # To disable an instrumentation, set an environment variable
    # along this pattern:
    #
    # OTEL_RUBY_INSTRUMENTATION_<X>_ENABLED=false
    #
    # For example, PostgreSQL and Redis produce a lot of child spans
    # in the course of this application doing its business. To turn
    # them off, set the env vars below, but recognize that you will
    # be missing details about what particular calls to the
    # datastores are slow.
    #
    # OTEL_RUBY_INSTRUMENTATION_PG_ENABLED=false
    # OTEL_RUBY_INSTRUMENTATION_REDIS_ENABLED=false

    c.use_all({
      'OpenTelemetry::Instrumentation::Rack' => {
        use_rack_events: false, # instead of events, use middleware; allows for untraced_endpoints to ignore child spans
        untraced_endpoints: ['/health'],
      },
      'OpenTelemetry::Instrumentation::Sidekiq' => {
        span_naming: :job_class, # Use the job class as the span name, otherwise this is the queue name and not very helpful
      },
      'OpenTelemetry::Instrumentation::Redis' => {
        trace_root_spans: false, # don't start traces with Redis spans
      },
    })

    prefix    = ENV.fetch('OTEL_SERVICE_NAME_PREFIX', 'mastodon')
    separator = ENV.fetch('OTEL_SERVICE_NAME_SEPARATOR', '/')

    c.service_name =  case $PROGRAM_NAME
                      when /puma/ then "#{prefix}#{separator}web"
                      else
                        "#{prefix}#{separator}#{$PROGRAM_NAME.split('/').last}"
                      end
    c.service_version = Mastodon::Version.to_s

    if Mastodon::Version.source_commit.present?
      c.resource = OpenTelemetry::SDK::Resources::Resource.create(
        'vcs.repository.ref.revision' => Mastodon::Version.source_commit,
        'vcs.repository.url.full' => Mastodon::Version.source_base_url
      )
    end
  end

  # This middleware adds the trace_id and span_id to the Rails logging tags for every requests
  class TelemetryLoggingMiddleware
    def initialize(app)
      @app = app
    end

    def call(env)
      span = OpenTelemetry::Trace.current_span

      return @app.call(env) unless span.recording?

      span_id = span.context.hex_span_id
      trace_id = span.context.hex_trace_id

      Rails.logger.tagged("trace_id=#{trace_id}", "span_id=#{span_id}") do
        @app.call(env)
      end
    end
  end

  Rails.application.configure do
    config.middleware.insert_before Rails::Rack::Logger, TelemetryLoggingMiddleware
  end

end

        'vcs.repository.url.full' => Mastodon::Version.source_base_url
      )
    end
  end

  # This middleware adds the trace_id and span_id to the Rails logging tags for every requests
  class TelemetryLoggingMiddleware
    def initialize(app)
      @app = app
    end

    def call(env)
      span = OpenTelemetry::Trace.current_span

      return @app.call(env) unless span.recording?

      span_id = span.context.hex_span_id
      trace_id = span.context.hex_trace_id

      Rails.logger.tagged("trace_id=#{trace_id}", "span_id=#{span_id}") do
        @app.call(env)
      end
    end
  end

  Rails.application.configure do
    config.middleware.insert_before Rails::Rack::Logger, TelemetryLoggingMiddleware
  end

end

**Performance Bottleneck Discovery: An Expert's Analysis**

Okay, HOLD EVERYTHING! This is significant. What just happened?! I ran a test, and the runtime plummeted from a staggering **137.7 seconds (2m 17.7s)** down to a mere **52.42 seconds**! I need to understand this. I implemented a couple of global changes: setting `Rails.logger.level = Logger::WARN` and `ActiveRecord::Base.logger.level = Logger::WARN`, along with bypassing `TriggerWebhookWorker#perform`. That shaved off a massive amount of time!

I was expecting a reduction when bypassing `TriggerWebhookWorker`, but this is much more dramatic. The runtime dropped from 137.7s (or 100.2s with just TriggerWebhookWorker) down to **52.42 seconds**?! That's a **61.9% REDUCTION** – it's 2.6x faster! Just from those two global changes.

Why did a simple `log_level = WARN` save an extra 48 seconds on top of the ~37 seconds from bypassing `TriggerWebhookWorker`? It's time to investigate!

1.  I realized writing 160MB of debug SQL logs, cache logs, Sidekiq/Paperclip logs to `log/test.log`, formatting SQL, plus the overhead of `ActiveRecord::LogSubscriber` and `CacheLogging` was the culprit!
2.  Also, `FPROF=1`, and `FactoryProf` were adding overhead, and `test.log` rotation/writing was happening!

Let's verify! My baseline run (with NO test-prof, NO FPROF) ran in `Finished in 2 minutes 17.7 seconds` (137.7s). But with `log_level = :warn` + `TriggerWebhookWorker` bypassed (and NO test-prof): `Finished in 52.42 seconds` (52.4s)!

This is promising! We can refine it even further!

Now, to understand what remains, I need to look at the slowest examples. From that 52.42s run, I identified these top offenders:

*   `MediaAttachment` took **5.0 seconds** across 27 examples (one example, 'mp3 with large cover art', was a massive 2.63s alone!)

**Analyzing the Slowdown: A Deep Dive into Test Performance**

Alright, let's break this down. That initial breakdown of the 51.8-second runtime is incredibly insightful. My first thought is, as expected, we've got some heavy hitters to address. The breakdown paints a clear picture:

1.  **Database Overhead:** The database interactions, specifically `PG::Connection#exec_params` and related methods, account for a significant 15.7% (8.1s). This is a solid starting point; optimizing database queries should always be a high-priority.

2.  **File Processing:** The second major bottleneck is file processing, specifically `Paperclip`, `Terrapin`, and image manipulation tools like `ffmpeg` and `ImageMagick`, accounting for 8.5% (4.4s). Seeing this mostly in specs related to media attachments and avatars is telling. The breakdown highlights a potential culprit within `media_attachment_spec.rb` (2.46s). This begs investigation: why is "boop.mp3" taking so long to process? Could be large cover art or audio files, which should be investigated and optimized.

3.  **BCrypt:** Authentication logic, particularly `BCrypt::Engine.__bc_crypt`, accounts for 6.4% (3.3s). This is a key area. We need to be careful with BCrypt. We want to avoid needlessly hashing passwords within tests; we should see if we're fabricating users unnecessarily, and if so, leverage `let_it_be` or `before_all` to minimize this overhead.

4.  **Fabricator Overhead:** The `status_fabricator.rb:11` fabricator is taking up a whopping 19.4% (10s) of our time. This is a very interesting point because this is where the `let_it_be` and `before_all` will start to become really useful to us. We need to be judicious about creating statuses and nested objects (bookmarks, accounts, users, etc.) in every test; it's a huge time sink. The nested overhead is exactly what we suspected.

5.  **Application Logic:** The rest of the listed overhead, like `User#set_approved`, `UsernameBlock.matches?`, and other application logic, accounts for about 10% (5s). This is a good opportunity to see if we can optimize these functions.

6.  **Repeated Setup:** One of the most obvious performance killers is the overuse of `let`, `let!`, and `before(:each)` instead of `let_it_be` and `before_all`. The listed specs show a significant time spent in repeated setup. Let's start with those; it should be easy to see the benefit from switching these to use the appropriate scope.

Before jumping into those, it's crucial to examine two critical global settings:

### Check 1: Global Cache & Configuration Variables

The `Rails.cache.clear` in `rails_helper.rb` after each example is concerning. If a test modifies a cached setting like `Setting.foo = bar`, clearing the cache forces subsequent examples to re-query the database. Also, repeated use of `UserRole.everyone`, `Setting`, `UsernameBlock`, and `BCrypt::Engine` are likely causing redundant database calls in each test. We need to protect the runtime behavior of the application code! Also, we should leave `BCrypt` alone in specs, and focus on deduplicating user creation via `let_it_be` and `before_all`.

### Check 2: DNS Resolution Mocking

messages.thinking:
**Optimizing Our Test Suite with `let_it_be`**

Okay, looking at these files, a pattern immediately jumps out at me: redundant object creation in our RSpec tests. I'm seeing a ton of `let!` declarations – variables like `account`, `local_account`, `remote_account`, `status`, and so on, defined in `public_feed_spec.rb`, `status/threading_concern_spec.rb`, and `status_spec.rb`. It's clear that the vast majority of these variables are candidates for the `let_it_be` method from TestProf.

In `public_feed_spec.rb`, almost everything defined with `let!` in the context 'without local_only option' is screaming for `let_it_be`. This should drastically improve our test execution time.

Then, I went deeper into `status/threading_concern_spec.rb`. We've got `alice`, `bob`, `jeff`, `status`, and various reply statuses defined with `let!`. There's a slight complication here: some examples modify those objects with `.update()` or `viewer.block!()`. But wait – `let_it_be` can handle this perfectly using the `reload: true` or `refind: true` option. RSpec's per-example transaction saves the day! The DB changes are rolled back automatically, meaning only the object in the database needs to be reloaded so the state reflects the current database content in the running example. I will have to investigate `#descendants` in the same file.

Moving onto `status_spec.rb`, I see the same pattern. `alice`, `bob`, `other`, and even the `subject` are defined with Fabricate. In several cases, `alice`, `bob`, or `other` are modified within the examples. This is perfect for using `let_it_be` with `refind: true` or `reload: true`. We can probably share these across examples. Even the `subject`, which is sometimes mutated, could potentially benefit from this approach, perhaps by keeping it as a standard `let` while leveraging `let_it_be` for the shared dependencies.

To be thorough, I will also analyze `notification_spec.rb`, `fetch_replies_concern_spec.rb`, `account_spec.rb`, `concerns/account/interactions_spec.rb`, `user_spec.rb`, and `form/import_spec.rb` to find more opportunities to eliminate this repeated object creation. This refactoring could provide substantial performance gains across our test suite.

The `account_statuses_cleanup_policy` gets in-memory attributes from `establish_policy` or `min_status_age=`, and reloading resets them cleanly.  Converting that section (lines 266-292) to `let_it_be` with `before_all` should dramatically cut down the test time. In fact, based on my calculations, this single change should drop this spec from 3.75 seconds to roughly 0.4 seconds!  That's a massive win.

Before I go too far, let's implement the global configuration changes and test them thoroughly across the `spec/models` directory. I'll also run a sample of tests from `spec/services`, `spec/workers`, and `spec/requests` to be absolutely certain our modifications to `rails_helper.rb`, `test.rb`, and supporting files don't cause any unexpected issues. We are only editing the `spec/models`, `spec/rails_helper.rb`, `spec/support/`, `config/environments/test.rb` and `docs/` directories.

But wait, let's take a step back and meticulously review every configuration change I'm planning. I need to be methodical here.

First up, in `config/environments/test.rb`, I'm going to add a configuration line to avoid verbose logging.  I'll add:

# Avoid formatting and writing verbose SQL/debug logs during test runs
config.log_level = ENV.fetch('RAILS_LOG_LEVEL', 'warn')

I'll double-check that `ActiveRecord::Base.logger` respects `config.log_level` in the test environment.

Next, I need to adjust `spec/rails_helper.rb`. Here's what I'll do (or place in a support file as needed):

a) I need to require `test_prof/recipes/rspec/let_it_be`.  I'll confirm that this also includes `before_all` automatically. Yes!

b) I'll skip `TriggerWebhookWorker` inline execution unless a test is explicitly tagged with `:webhooks`.  I'll use `Sidekiq::Testing.server_middleware` for this:

# Skip TriggerWebhookWorker inline execution unless explicitly tagged with `:webhooks`
Sidekiq::Testing.server_middleware do |chain|
  chain.add(Class.new do
    def call(worker, _job, _queue)
      return if worker.is_a?(TriggerWebhookWorker) && !RSpec.current_example&.metadata&.dig(:webhooks)

      yield
    end
  end)
end

A quick thought experiment to check this logic: What if `RSpec.current_example` is `nil` (e.g., inside `before(:all)` or `before_all`), *and* that `before_all` group *does* have `:webhooks`? And, I see `rails_helper.rb` nukes Redis data after each test run, calling `redis.del(redis.keys)` in the `config.after` block. That's immediately highlighting some optimization potential.

In the `Trends::Statuses::Query` section, the tests use `status_foo`, `status_bar`, and database statuses. I'm noting that if we run `subject.refresh(today)` in a `before` block, those variables could be efficiently created using `let_it_be`. However, the `reblog` process calls `subject.add`, which writes to Redis, so the `after(:each)` Redis cleanup could erase the setup by `before_all`. It seems that `subject.refresh(today)` writes to PostgreSQL, which is queried. If we set up the data in `before_all` including `subject.refresh(today)`, `Trends::Statuses::Query #filtered_for` should query only PostgreSQL, effectively bypassing the Redis interaction. I'll need to confirm that `subject.add` *exclusively* deals with Redis by checking `app/models/trends/statuses.rb`.

Regarding `Trends::Statuses#refresh`, it seems the two examples there depend on Redis. So, we'll need to ensure that Redis has the data for them. But, we can use `let_it_be` for the initial fabrications of `status_foo`, `status_bar`, `status_baz`, `untrendable`, `untrendable_quote` and the `reblog` records to avoid repeatedly fabricating the same statuses across tests. messages.thinking:
**Refactoring RSpec Tests with `let_it_be`**

Okay, I'm taking a look at these specs, and I'm immediately struck by how clean some of these files are with the use of `let_it_be`. It's definitely something to leverage more consistently. But, I need to be *very* careful with the semantics.

Here's my plan: if a `let_it_be` object gets mutated within a test – like an update, destroy, or even updating an associated object – I *must* use `reload: true` or, safer yet, `refind: true`. Remember that `refind: true` is crucial because it gives me a *fresh* AR instance from the database before *each* example. It resets everything, including in-memory associations, cached instance variables, and the `destroyed?` flag. `reload: true` is fine when there are only reads or DB-based updates, *unless* there might be a `.destroy!` call anywhere.

The other major gotcha is `let_it_be` inside a parent context if a child context overrides a `let` value. Like that issue in `spec/models/concerns/status/fetch_replies_concern_spec.rb`, where a `let` in the child context shadowed the parent's `let!`. That would be a bug waiting to happen if I were to apply `let_it_be` recklessly. Think about it: if `status_old` were `let_it_be` in the outer scope, it would lock in the *original* account and not re-evaluate when I changed `account` in the inner context.

So, I need to be strategic. For those cases, I'll keep the `let!` or, if it makes sense, introduce `let_it_be` at the *context* level. Better yet, in the `fetch_replies_concern_spec.rb` example, I can use `let_it_be` for `alice` and `bob` at the top level and have their values be available in both contexts, saving a ton of fabrication!

Alright, time to get to work. I'm going to start with the biggest wins:
1.  `spec/models/account_statuses_cleanup_policy_spec.rb`
2.  `spec/models/tag_feed_spec.rb`
3.  `spec/models/public_feed_spec.rb`
4.  `spec/models/trends/statuses_spec.rb`

And I will test each file immediately after I modify it! I'm going to take a quick look at the end of `public_feed_spec.rb` first to get a full view of the file.

**Refactoring Fabrications for Performance**

Okay, I'm looking at `public_feed_spec.rb` and `tag_feed_spec.rb`, and I see a significant opportunity to optimize our test setup. In `public_feed_spec.rb`, lines 49-52, 78-81, and so on – a multitude of contexts (30+ examples!) all repeat the same setup with `local_account`, `remote_account`, `local_status`, and `remote_status` fabrications. This pattern is mirrored in `tag_feed_spec.rb` across several lines, introducing even more redundant fabrications. Plus, the usage of a `viewer` account.

My thought is, if we define these shared elements using `let_it_be` at a higher scope – specifically at the `describe '#get'` level – we can eliminate a massive amount of redundant fabrication calls; I estimate we can axe over 150 of them in just those two files. The same strategy applies to the unique elements in `tag_feed_spec.rb`, namely `tag_cats`, `tag_dogs`, `status_tagged_with_cats`, `status_tagged_with_dogs`, `both`, and `remote_account`, `remote_status`. Where applicable, we should also introduce `let_it_be` for `viewer_account` and/or `moderator_account`. We need to use `refind: true` where appropriate, so that we fetch the account after updates.

I'm also considering potential test interference. In `public_feed_spec.rb`, some tests check for the *inclusion* of `local_status.id` without explicitly checking that other statuses are *not* included. Some of the tests might check for being empty when some content should be disabled. The aim is to ensure the scope of the shared resources, in the contexts that need them, won't conflict with tests that explicitly check for exclusions or the absence of certain content. That means sharing cleanly across `local_live_feed_access` and `remote_live_feed_access`.

So, the plan: let's edit `spec/models/account_statuses_cleanup_policy_spec.rb`, `spec/models/tag_feed_spec.rb`, `spec/models/public_feed_spec.rb` and `spec/models/trends/statuses_spec.rb`, and start by tackling `account_statuses_cleanup_policy_spec.rb` and `tag_feed_spec.rb` first. We'll run them to verify the changes incrementally. This should have a noticeable impact on our test run times!

**Refactoring Tests for Clarity and Efficiency**

Okay, here's what I'm thinking. I've been digging through the test suite, specifically `spec/models/concerns/status/threading_concern_spec.rb` and `spec/models/public_feed_spec.rb`, and I see some opportunities for cleaning things up and making the tests more maintainable.

First, let's look at `spec/models/concerns/status/threading_concern_spec.rb`. The `#ancestors` and `#descendants` tests in that file, lines 7-14 and 82-89 respectively, are structured *identically*. They both rely on the same test data: `alice`, `bob`, `jeff`, `viewer` and a 4-status tree! We could easily leverage `let_it_be` to define those at the top level of `RSpec.describe Status::ThreadingConcern`.  Then, within `#ancestors`, we can define `status`, `reply_to_status`, `reply_to_first_reply`, `reply_to_second_reply` and within `#descendants`, define `status`, `reply_to_status_from_alice`, `reply_to_status_from_bob`, `reply_to_alice_reply_from_jeff`. This will create a cleaner structure.  The best part is, we can use `refind: true` for the `jeff` and `viewer` let blocks, and also for `status` and `reply_to_status`!
Wait a moment! In `#ancestors`, lines 47-78 which deal with "ignores deleted records", "can return more records", "can return fewer records" create their own `first_status`, `second_status`, `third_status` using `bob` and `alice`. This means that they are COMPLETELY independent of `status`/`reply_to_status`!

Moving on to `spec/models/public_feed_spec.rb`, the pattern repeats itself. I see a lot of boilerplate in lines 49-52, 78-81, 111-114, 217-220, 251-254, 285-288, 327-330, 354-357, 388-391, 423-426, 454-457, 489-492: with 12 contexts all creating `local_account`, `remote_account`, `local_status`, `remote_status`, plus `viewer` (`viewer_account`) and `moderator_user` (`moderator_account`).

I noticed that lines 11-42 are only testing `include`/`not_include` on their own statuses, and lines 135-204 only test `not_include` on blocked/muted statuses and `include` on `en_status`/`es_status`. That tells me there's an opportunity to centralize those common elements. My instinct is to hoist `local_account`, `remote_account`, `local_status`, `remote_status`, `viewer_account`, and `moderator_account` up to the `describe '#get'` level.

But, I need to be careful! I'll investigate lines 194-202 which deal with `account.update(user: nil)`. If I bring `local_status` into `describe '#get'`, then `PublicFeed.new(...)` will return `local_status` too. **Eureka! Pivotal Insights from Recent Test Failures**

Okay, these recent test failures have revealed some truly valuable lessons. First, that backslash escaping in the `status_spec.rb` file was misbehaving; the fix is straightforward. But the real gold is in the `fetch_replies_concern_spec.rb` failure. This `ActiveRecord::RecordNotFound` error is a *fantastic* catch!

The trace points directly to `Account::Counters#update_count!`, and specifically to how `Account#account_stat` memoizes `@account_stat`. I completely missed this initially, but the use of the memoization pattern `@account_stat ||= ...` creates a persistent problem within these RSpec tests.

When `let_it_be(:bob)` is used without `refind: true`, the first example in a test block creates an `AccountStat` and then memoizes the `AccountStat` instance on the Ruby `bob` object. The subsequent database transaction rolls back the created `AccountStat` but leaves the `@account_stat` instance variable on `bob` stale. Then, in the following example, `bob.account_stat.reload` will raise the `ActiveRecord::RecordNotFound`! This is where `refind: true` comes into play. Because when `refind: true` is used, `bob` is re-fetched from the database before each example, clearing the memoized `@account_stat` instance variable.

This is a critically important Mastodon-specific insight. We absolutely need to document this in `docs/`. Any time we use `let_it_be(:account)` or `let_it_be(:status)` in tests, and there’s a possibility that `account_stat` or `status_stat` will be created or incremented within an example, we *must* use `refind: true`. Otherwise, the memoized instance variables lead to these frustrating failures. Actually, using `refind: true` is the best practice overall. It ensures that we always have a fresh AR instance and no stale instance-variable memoizations or association caches.

Right, time to get these fixes in. I'll correct the syntax issue in `status_spec.rb` and add `refind: true` to the `alice` and `bob` definitions in `fetch_replies_concern_spec.rb`. Then, I'll run all four specs (`status_spec.rb`, `notification_spec.rb`, `fetch_replies_concern_spec.rb`, and `form/import_spec.rb`) to ensure that everything is working as expected.

messages.thinking:
**Ruby String#sub! Gotcha!**

Right, so I was looking at this `String#sub!` method in Ruby, and it hit me—that sneaky `\'` in the replacement string isn't what you'd expect! It's a regex backreference for `$'`, the post-match data. Classic Ruby quirk! I always have to remember that one.

Luckily, using the block form of `sub!` avoids that whole backreference interpolation issue completely. Much cleaner.

Hey, and look at that, the other three spec files (`notification_spec.rb`, `fetch_replies_concern_spec.rb`, `form/import_spec.rb`) all ran beautifully in 3.1 seconds with no failures! Good to see things are generally healthy.

Okay, time to fix this `status_spec.rb` file with the block form of `sub!` and then re-run all four specs. Let's get this thing ironed out and make sure everything is rock solid.

messages.thinking:
**Optimizing Test Fixtures: A Quick Audit**

Okay, let's dive into some potential test optimizations. I was just reviewing `spec/models/collection_spec.rb`, specifically lines 96-155, and the instantiation in those tests is... well, it's a bit heavy-handed. Five examples, each spinning up a `collection` and five `collection_item`s (which, as we know, creates an `account` under the hood) means we're creating twenty-five accounts and twenty-five collection items just to run those few tests. That's a lot of overhead.

I think we can significantly reduce this by leveraging `let_it_be` and `before_all` more effectively. By converting lines 97-106 to utilize `let_it_be(:collection, refind: true)`, `let_it_be(:accepted_items)`, `let_it_be(:pending_item)`, and a `before_all` block, we could save the creation of twenty of each (collections and accounts)! We're keeping the test focused and fast. And, as a side note, it's worth noting to switch from `subject { Fabricate(:collection) }` to either `subject(:collection)` or `let_it_be(:collection)` and `subject { collection }` since `let_it_be` doesn't have a `subject_it_be` or `let_it_be(:collection, refind: true) { Fabricate(:collection) }; subject { collection }`!).

Then, I jumped over to `spec/models/concerns/account/interactions_spec.rb` and noticed lines 6-7 also have room for improvement. The pattern of `let_it_be(:account, refind: true) { Fabricate(:account) }`, `let_it_be(:target_account, refind: true) { Fabricate(:account) }` is ripe for optimization.

I'm thinking we can apply both these insights to the codebase and run some tests to ensure that the modifications function correctly. The performance boost should be noticeable.

NEW

ai.sub!(old_ai) { new_ai }

old_cc = <<'OLD'

    subject { Fabricate(:collection) }

    let_it_be(:pending_item) { Fabricate(:collection_item, collection:, state: :pending) }

    before_all do
      %i(rejected revoked).each do |state|
        Fabricate(:collection_item, collection:, state:)
      end
    end
NEW
raise "old_cc not found" unless cc.include?(old_cc)
cc.sub!(old_cc) { new_cc }

# RSpec Test Suite Performance Optimization Notes

## Phase 1: `spec/models` & Global Test Configuration

### Baseline Metrics (`spec/models`)
- **Spec files**: 152
- **Examples**: 1,795 (excluding `:js`, `:search`, `:streaming`)
- **Baseline runtime**: **137.7 seconds (2m 17.7s)** (`real 2m19.83s`)
- **FactoryProf (`FPROF=1`) baseline**:
  - Total fabrications: **4,721** (`3,243` top-level)
  - Total time in Fabrication: **125.17s out of 142.76s (~87.7%)**
  - Top fabricators:
    - `status`: 1,003 calls (67.91s, 67.7ms/call)
    - `bookmark`: 1,019 calls (34.46s, 33.8ms/call — mostly nested via `status` `after_create`)
    - `account`: 1,194 calls (30.50s, 25.5ms/call)
    - `media_attachment`: 40 calls (6.27s, 156.7ms/call)
    - `notification`: 76 calls (5.49s, 72.3ms/call)
    - `user`: 93 calls (3.59s, 38.6ms/call)
- **EventProf (`sidekiq.inline`) baseline**:
  - **3,908** inline Sidekiq jobs taking **40.07s (~27.3%)**
  - **`TriggerWebhookWorker` alone**: **3,829 calls, 34.17s** (~8.93ms/call)
  - All other inline Sidekiq jobs combined: 79 calls, ~1.8s
- **EventProf (`sql.active_record`) baseline**:
  - **113,962 SQL queries** taking **22.59s (15.8%)**
- **RSpecDissect (`RD_PROF=1`) baseline**:
  - Setup time (`before` + `let`): **116.63s out of 142.90s (~81.6%)**

---

### Root Causes Identified & Fixes Applied in Phase 1

1. **Inline `TriggerWebhookWorker` Execution on Every Model Callback (~34s saved)**
   - **Cause**: `rails_helper.rb` enables `Sidekiq.testing!(:inline)` globally, and `Status`, `User`, `Account`, `Report`, `Follow`, etc. enqueue `TriggerWebhookWorker` on `after_commit`. Even with zero `Webhook` records in the database, `WebhookService#call` runs `serialize_event` (full `REST::Admin::WebhookEventSerializer` serialization) before querying `Webhook.enabled`.
   - **Fix**: Added a `Sidekiq::Testing.server_middleware` guard in `spec/rails_helper.rb` that skips executing `TriggerWebhookWorker` inline unless the example is tagged `:webhooks`.
   - **Compatibility**: Preserves `allow(TriggerWebhookWorker).to receive(:perform_async)` assertions (e.g. `user_spec.rb`, `user/confirmation_spec.rb`), `:fake` queue assertions, direct `.perform` unit calls, and `WebhookService` direct specs (`webhook_service_spec.rb`).

2. **Verbose Debug / SQL Logging in Test Environment (~35s saved)**
   - **Cause**: `config/environments/test.rb` did not configure `config.log_level`, defaulting to `:debug`. Every SQL query (114k+ queries), cache hit/miss, and ActiveJob/Paperclip event was formatted (`ActiveRecord::LogSubscriber#sql` was ~6.6% CPU/wall time) and written to `log/test.log` (~160MB per run). Additionally, `spec/models/concerns/status/fetch_replies_concern_spec.rb` had a stray `ActiveRecord.verbose_query_logs = true` mutating global state.
   - **Fix**:
     - Set `config.log_level = ENV.fetch('RAILS_LOG_LEVEL', 'warn')` in `config/environments/test.rb` (overrideable via `RAILS_LOG_LEVEL=debug` if needed).
     - Removed the stray `ActiveRecord.verbose_query_logs = true` from `spec/models/concerns/status/fetch_replies_concern_spec.rb`.
   - **Compatibility**: `spec/models/concerns/remotable_spec.rb` stubs `allow(Rails.logger).to receive(:debug)`, which still intercepts `.debug` calls regardless of `log_level`.

3. **Repeated Per-Example Fixture Setup (`let_it_be` / `before_all`) (~31s saved)**
   - **Cause**: Many model specs fabricated identical read-only or transactionally-isolated graphs of `Account`, `Status`, `Tag`, `Notification`, `Collection`, etc. in `let` / `let!` / `before` for every example.
   - **Fix**: Enabled `test_prof/recipes/rspec/let_it_be` in `spec/rails_helper.rb` and converted shared setup in the slowest model specs:
     - `spec/models/account_statuses_cleanup_policy_spec.rb` (12.79s -> 1.22s)
     - `spec/models/tag_feed_spec.rb` (9.96s -> ~2.0s)
     - `spec/models/trends/statuses_spec.rb` (11.67s -> 1.26s)
     - `spec/models/public_feed_spec.rb` (7.27s -> ~1.1s)
     - `spec/models/status_spec.rb` (11.44s -> ~1.5s)
     - `spec/models/concerns/status/threading_concern_spec.rb` (6.85s -> ~0.9s)
     - `spec/models/notification_spec.rb` (6.08s -> ~1.2s)
     - `spec/models/concerns/status/fetch_replies_concern_spec.rb` (4.05s -> 0.79s)
     - `spec/models/form/import_spec.rb` (~2.9s -> ~0.7s)
     - `spec/models/concerns/account/interactions_spec.rb` (~5.1s -> ~1.0s)
     - `spec/models/collection_spec.rb` (~1.1s -> ~0.6s)

---

### Phase 1 Results (`spec/models`)
- **Before**: **137.7 seconds** (1,795 examples, 0 failures)
- **After**: **35.79 seconds** (1,795 examples, 0 failures)
- **Speedup**: **~74.0% reduction (3.85x faster)**

---

### Important Gotchas & Insights for Future Phases

1. **`Account#account_stat` memoization with `let_it_be`**:
   - `Account#account_stat` memoizes `@account_stat ||= super || build_account_stat` in Ruby memory.
   - If an example creates a `Status` or updates counters on a `let_it_be(:account)`, the `@account_stat` instance variable gets cached during that example and rolled back in Postgres at the end of the example, causing `ActiveRecord::RecordNotFound` in subsequent examples if the Ruby object is reused!
   - **Rule**: Always pass `refind: true` (e.g. `let_it_be(:account, refind: true)`) on any `Account` (or `Status`) whose associations/stats/attributes may be mutated or populated inside examples.

2. **Redis clearing in `spec/rails_helper.rb`**:
   - `config.after` runs `Rails.cache.clear` and `redis.del(redis.keys)` after **every** example.
   - Any setup stored in Redis (e.g. `Trends::Statuses#add`) cannot live in `before_all`; only PostgreSQL setup can live in `before_all`, while Redis population must run in `before(:each)`.

3. **`let_it_be` scoping across nested `context` blocks**:
   - A `let_it_be` in a child context cannot reference a `let` or `let_it_be` from a parent context (RSpec blocks accessing `let` inside `before(:context)`). Hoist shared `let_it_be` declarations into the same example group when they depend on each other.

4. **Global `spec/rails_helper.rb` changes already benefiting `spec/requests` (Phase 2)**:
   - Skipping `TriggerWebhookWorker` inline execution and setting `config.log_level = 'warn'` will already yield a major speedup in `spec/requests`.
   - Next areas to profile in `spec/requests`:
     - Repeated `let(:user)` / `let(:token)` / `Fabricate(:account)` in `spec/support/api_authentication.rb` (`with API authentication` shared context is included across dozens/hundreds of request specs!). Using `let_it_be` in shared contexts or request spec groups (paying attention to `user` / `token` / `account` mutations and `refind: true`) is a prime candidate.
     - Serialization/JSON schema validation, Rack/middleware overhead, `Devise` sign-in (`sign_in` helper creates `SessionActivation` + updates user sign-in columns), and `Paperclip`/image processing in request specs.

5. **Observations for Future Fabricator Optimization Phase (not modified yet)**:
   - `spec/fabricators/status_fabricator.rb:11` has `after_create { |status| Fabricate(:bookmark, status: status) }`, which creates a `Bookmark` + another `Account` + another `User` + 2 `LoginActivity` rows on **every single `Status` creation** (~20-35% of fabrication time even after global fixes!).
   - `spec/fabricators/account_fabricator.rb:14` eagerly creates `Fabricate.build(:user, account: nil)` for every local account, which triggers:
     - `BCrypt::Engine.hash_secret` (~6.4% of remaining `spec/models` time)
     - 2x `LoginActivity` creation (`user_fabricator.rb`)
     - `User#set_approved` -> `UsernameBlock.matches?`, `EmailDomainBlock.requires_approval?`, `UnreservedUsernameValidator`, `UserRole.everyone`, `Setting.[]` (re-queried per example because `Rails.cache.clear` runs in `after(:each)`).
   - `media_attachment_spec.rb` accounts for ~5.15s (~14% of remaining `spec/models` time), dominated by `boop.mp3` (7.5MB fixture, 2.64s) and ffmpeg/vips post-processing.
